docs.text: Determine the desire to charge Whether a user wants to charge depends on the current battery charge level, the user's charge and stop triggers, and, where applicable, the charging price. Three regions are distinguished: At or below the charge trigger , the user wants to charge irrespective of the charging price. At or above the stop trigger , the user does not want to charge, irrespective of the charging price. Between the charge and stop triggers , the decision depends on the balance between the user's charging need and the charging price. The charging need describes how strongly a user wants to charge at a given battery charge level. For battery proportion \(b\) , charge trigger \(b_t\) , and stop trigger \(b_s\) , the charging need between the two triggers is \[ N(b) = \frac{b_s - b}{b - b_t}. \] The charging need increases as the battery level approaches the charge trigger and approaches zero as the battery level approaches the stop trigger. At the midpoint between the two triggers, \[ b = \frac{b_t + b_s}{2}, \] the charging need is equal to one: \[ N(b) = 1. \] Above the charge trigger, the charging need is compared with the price pain. The price pain is the actual charging price \(p\) relative to the user's reference price \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}\) : \[ P = \frac{p}{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}. \] The user wants to charge when the charging need is at least as large as the price pain: \[ N(b) \geq P. \] Equivalently, the maximum charging price that the user is willing to pay at a given battery charge level is \[ p_{\max}(b) = p_{\mathrm{ref}} \frac{b_s - b}{b - b_t}. \] This is the boundary shown by the black curve in the figure. Below the curve, the charging price is sufficiently low and the user wants to charge. Above the curve, the user does not want to charge. The reference price therefore has a direct interpretation. When the actual charging price is equal to the reference price, \[ p = p_{\mathrm{ref}}, \] the user is just willing to charge at the midpoint between the charge and stop triggers. A reference price of zero disables price-sensitive charging. In that case, the user wants to charge only when the battery level is at or below the charge trigger. This reproduces threshold-only charging behaviour. For normal charging, the charging decision is evaluated at the start of a charging session. If the user decides to charge, the decision is not reevaluated as the battery level rises during that session. Charging continues until the stop level is reached. Consequently, the charging decision is based on the charging price at the start of the session; subsequent price changes during the same session do not causee charging-desire formulation is used for fast charging, using separate fast-charging charge and stop triggers, charging prices, and reference prices. Setting the fast-charging reference price to zero restricts fast charging to the automatic fast-charge trigger. A small positive fast-charging reference price allows sufficiently attractive fast-charging prices to trigger fast charging above the automatic trigger as well.

There is one per scenario, containing all necessary parameters to run the scenario. To add a scenario, copy one of the existing files and add/remove/modify parameters as required, including the first parameter, which is the scenario name, which should be the same as the file name (it might work with another name, but this is not tested and there is no reason to have different names for the same scenario). These scenario files contain the following sections: - unit_conversions: Parameters to convert units - files: File-related parameters (folders, output type choices, etc.) - colors: Color-related parameters(defining new ones, as well as color bars) - time: Time-related parameters and constants needed in formulas - run: Parameters related to the run, such as timing, and elements such as locations, vehicles, legs, trips, etc. - weather: Parameters related to the weather, such as elements to define what we want to download from various sources, where we store weather data, how we process it, or how we want to label quantities - plots: Parameters for plots (colors, sizes, etc.) define.py: This module defines and declares classes for the different objects that define the system (the parameters/defintions come from a parameters file), namely: 1. Legs: Legs are point-to-point vehicle movements (i.e. movements where the vehicle goes from a start location and ends/stops at an end location). 2. Vehicles: Each vehicle type (or subtype) is defined in this class. weather.py This module contains functions related to weather data and factors. The weather data is pulled from the CDS (Climate Data Store) ERA-5 weather data from the Copernicus institute . This data contains many quantities (such as temperature, precipitation, or solar radiation) at an hourly level (starting in 1950) for the whole world, at a one-decimal resolution for latitudes and longitudes. Note that the data sometimes has trailing digits, but the resolution still seems to be to the first decimal. This is the reason why we round the coordinate values in our processing functions. It contains the following functions: 1. download_cds_weather_quantity: Downloads CDS ERA-5 weather data for a given quantity in a given area. 2. download_all_cds_weather_data: Downloads all the necessary CDS weather data. 3. make_weather_dataframe: This function makes a weather DataFrame into one we can use by removing empty data and processing data into forms useful for the model. 4. write_weather_database" This function writes the weather database. 5. get_hourly_values: This function takes a Dataframe for a given weather quantity. If this is a cumulative quantity, it adds hourly values to it. 6. get_all_hourly_values: This functions adds hourly values to cumulative quantities in the weather database. 7. get_EV_tool_data: : This gets the temperature efficiency data from the EV tool made by geotab . 8. temperature_efficiency_factor: This function returns the temperature efficiency factor that corrects the baseline vehicle efficiency. 9. plot_temperature_efficiency: Plots the temperature efficiency correction factor (source data versus interpolation)of electric vehicles. 10. get_run_location_weather_quantity: Returns a chosen weather quantity for a given location and a given runtime. 11. get_run_weather_data: Fetches the weather data and efficiency factors and puts it into a table that is saved to files/databases. 12. solar_efficiency_factor: * This gives us the efficiency factor of solar panels (i.e. how much of the solar radiation is converted into electricity). THIS IS A PLACEHOLDER FUNCTION 13. setup_weather: This runs all the functions necessary to get the run weather factors for a given case. 14. get_location_weather_quantity: Returns the value a a chosen weather quantity for a given location and time tag. run_time.py: This module defines time structures. It contains the following functions: 1. get_time_range: This function returns the time range of the run, and the associated hour numbers, based on values found in the parameters file. 2. get_time_stamped_dataframe: This function creates a DataFrame with the timestamps of the run as index (and hour numbers as a column). 3. get_day_type: Tells us the date type of a given time_tag. 4. add_day_type_to_time_stamped_dataframe: Adds a column with the date type to a time-stamped_dataframe writing.py: This contains functions related to writting outputs. It contains the following functions: 1. write_scenario_parameters: This function writes the scenario parameters to the output files (either as separate files, or as tables/sheets in groupfiles.) mobility.py: This module computes the various functions related to mobility. It contains the following functions: 1. get_trip_probabilities_per_day_type: This function computes the trip probabilities per day type. Temperature efficiency This function returns the temperature efficiency factor that corrects the baseline vehicle efficiency. It uses a data file (extracted from EV tool made by geotab . This information is based on 5.2 million trips by 4200 vehicles. The degree 6 polynomial fit is: \[ C(T)=0.7078+0.01751\cdot T+0.0001611\cdot T^2-1.036\cdot 10^{-5}\cdot T^3 -3.581\cdot 10^{-7}\cdot T^4+1.746\cdot 10^{-9}\cdot T^5 +1.07\cdot10^{-10}\cdot T^6 \] where T is the ambient temparture (in the weather data, it's the temperature at 2 meters), and C is the efficiency correction factor. docs.text: Classes Leg This class defines the legs and their properties, from a scenario file that contains a list of instances and their properties. Legs are point-to-point vehicle movements (i.e. movements where the vehicle goes from a start location and ends/stops at an end location). Parameters The parameters of a leg are: Name: The name of the leg Vehicle: The vehicle that runs the leg. If this does not correspond to the scenario vehicle name , then the leg is not declared. Note that when running a scenario, you select one vehicle, so this is in principle not necessary. The reason for having this is to allow the user to copy the baseline file and keep the location definitions that are not used for this scenario but might be so for another, thereby reducing the need for changes between scenarios. Distance: The distance driven during the leg (in kilometers) Duration: How long it takes to drive the leg (in hours) Hour in day factors: These factors add a correction to the vehicle consumption that depend on the hour in day (the first is for 00:00 to 00:59, last for 23:00 to 23:59). Note that these are actual hours, not hours in the user day (which can start and end at other moments than midnight). This is used to take into account things like traffic jams. The default value is 1. This factor is a placeholder and is currently not in use. Location This class defines the locations where the vehicles are and their properties, from a scenario file that contains a list of instances and their proper. Parameters The parameters of a location are: Name : The name of the location. Vehicle: The vehicle that uses the location. If this does not correspond to the scenario vehicle name , then the trip is not declared. Note that when running a scenario, you select one vehicle, so this is in principle not necessary. The reason for having this is to allow the user to copy the baseline file and keep the location definitions that are not used for this scenario but might be so for another, thereby reducing the need for changes between scenarios. Connectivity: A value between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%) that tells the probability that a vehicle parked at this location is connected to a charger. Charging power: The (peak) charging power of the charger at this location (in kW). Charger efficiency: A value between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%) that tells how much of the power drawn from the network is delivered to the battery of the vehicle. Latitude: The latitude of the location. This factor is a placeholder and is currently not in use. Longitude: The longitude of the location. This factor is a placeholder and is currently not in use. Base charging price: The base/reference (i.e. before flexibility/temporal changes) charging price at this location, in €/kWh. This factor is a placeholder and is currently not in use. Charging desirability: A value between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%) that tells how much the users like to charge at this location. This factor is a placeholder and is currently not in use. Percentage in location at run start: A value between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%) that tells which percentage of the vehicles start the run there. This is used if we will that in directly instead of computing it. The decision t use this is controlled by the compute_start_location_split parameter in the mobility module. Trip This class defines the trips and their properties, from a scenario file that contains a list of instances and their properties. Trips are collections of legs that take place on a given day. Note that this day does not necessarily start (and end) at midnight, but can start (and end) at an hour that is more logical/significant for the vehicle user (it could for example be 05:00 for car drivers). This day start hour parameter is universal for all trips This value is set in the scenario files. Parameters Name : The name of the trip. Vehicle: The vehicle that does the trip. If this does not correspond to the scenario vehicle name , then the trip is not declared. Note that when running a scenario, you select one vehicle, so this is in principle not necessary. The reason for having this is to allow the user to copy the baseline file and keep the trip definitions that are not used for this scenario but might be so for another, thereby reducing the need for changes between scenarios. Legs: A list of the legs in the trip. Time between legs: A list of the time spent at the arrival locations between each leg (in hours). Percentage station users: A value between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%) that tells us which percentage of users use fast charging stations. This factor is a placeholder and is currently not in use. Start probabilities: A list of values between 0 and 1 (0%-100%) adding up to 1/100% that tells us what the probability of starting the trip is at a given hour. Note that the hours start at day start hour , not at midnight. Repeated sequence: A list of repeated legs (which should follow each other) that form a repeated sequence. Repetition amounts: How often the repeated sequence is repeated. This is a list, with one value per leg repetition (the nth element corresponds to the nth appearance of the sequence in the leg list). Time between repetitions: The time between repetitions of each repeated sequence (in hours). This is a list, with one value per leg repetition (the nth element corresponds to the nth appearance of the sequence in the leg list). Mobility matrix The main aim of the trip initialization/declaration is to create a mobility matrix for the trip. This mobility matrix has, for all combinations of possible start and end locations (i.e. locations connected by a leg in the trip) and for each hour in day number (starting at the day start hour ), the following quantities: 1. Duration: The duration (in hours) of a leg between the start location and the end location. 2. Distance: The distance (in kilometers) of a leg between the start location. 3. Weighted distance: The weighted distance (in kilometers) of a leg between the start location and the end location. This corresponds to using different road types , with given weights and given mixes to account for the fact that vehicles consume more on some road types. 4. Departures amount : The chance that a vehicle, in a given hour, leaves the start location, going to the end location (amount and chance are equivalent here, as we compute on an individual vehicle basis). 5. Departures kilometers: The kilometers driven by vehicles leaving the start location at a given hour and going to the end location. This is given by the departures amount times the distance. 6. Departures weighted kilometers: The weighted (by road type) kilometers driven by vehicles leaving the start location at a given hour and going to the end location. This is given by the departures amount times the weighted distance. 7. Arrivals amount : The chance that a vehicle, in a given hour, arrives to the end location, having started the start location (amount and chance are equivalent here, as we compute on an individual vehicle basis). 8. Arrivals kilometers: The kilometers driven by vehicles arriving to the end location at a given hour, having started at the start location. This is given by the arrivals amount times the distance. 9. Arrivals weighted kilometers: The weighted (by road type) kilometers driven by vehicles arriving to the end location at a given hour, having started at the start location. This is given by the arrivals amount times the weighted distance. The model also produces a version of this mobility matrix for the whole run (which is essentially a copy of the above matrix). This run mobility matrix is the mobility matrix if the trip had a probability of 1 for the whole run. Leg repetitions Is repeat of leg or two legs???? [0, 5, 5, 0] If next leg is also repeated/still has repeats left, then it is repeated after the leg in question so when putting a leg, check if it is repeated. If so, check if the next is repeated, until you have no repeats (or end the list). Parameters The parameters of a leg are: Name: The name of the leg Vehicle: The vehicle that runs the leg. If this does not correspond to the scenario vehicle name , then the leg is not declared. Note that when running a scenario, you select one vehicle, so this is in principle not necessary. The reason for having this is to allow the user to copy the baseline file and keep the location definitions that are not used for this scenario but might be so for another, thereby reducing the need for changes between scenarios. Distance: The distance driven during the leg (in kilometers) Duration: How long it takes to drive the leg (in hours) Hour in day factors: These factors add a correction to the vehicle consumption that depend on the hour in day (the first is for 00:00 to 00:59, last for 23:00 to 23:59). Note that these are actual hours, not hours in the user day (which can start and end at other moments than midnight). This is used to take into account things like traffic jams. The default value is 1. This factor is a placeholder and is currently not in use. Location This class defines the locations where the vehicles are and their properties, from a scenario file that contains a list of instances and their proper. Parameters The parameters of a location are: Name : The name of the location. Vehicle: The vehicle that uses the location. If this does not correspond to the scenario vehicle name , then the trip is not declared. Note that when running a scenario, you select one vehicle, so this is in principle not necessary. The reason for having this is to allow the user to copy the baseline file and keep the location definitions that are not used for this scenario but might be so for another, thereby reducing the need for changes between scenarios. Connectivity: A value between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%) that tells the probability that a vehicle parked at this location is connected to a charger. Charging power: The (peak) charging power of the charger at this location (in kW). Charger efficiency: A value between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%) that tells how much of the power drawn from the network is delivered to the battery of the vehicle. Latitude: The latitude of the location. This factor is a placeholder and is currently not in use. Longitude: The longitude of the location. This factor is a placeholder and is currently not in use. Base charging price: The base/reference (i.e. before flexibility/temporal changes) charging price at this location, in €/kWh. This factor is a placeholder and is currently not in use. Charging desirability: A value between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%) that tells how much the users like to charge at this location. This factor is a placeholder and is currently not in use. Percentage in location at run start: A value between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%) that tells which percentage of the vehicles start the run there. This is used if we will that in directly instead of computing it. The decision t use this is controlled by the compute_start_location_split parameter in the mobility module. Trip This class defines the trips and their properties, from a scenario file that contains a list of instances and their properties. Trips are collections of legs that take place on a given day. Note that this day does not necessarily start (and end) at midnight, but can start (and end) at an hour that is more logical/significant for the vehicle user (it could for example be 05:00 for car drivers). This day start hour parameter is universal for all trips This value is set in the scenario files. Parameters Name : The name of the trip. Vehicle: The vehicle that does the trip. If this does not correspond to the scenario vehicle name , then the trip is not declared. Note that when running a scenario, you select one vehicle, so this is in principle not necessary. The reason for having this is to allow the user to copy the baseline file and keep the trip definitions that are not used for this scenario but might be so for another, thereby reducing the need for changes between scenarios. Legs: A list of the legs in the trip. Time between legs: A list of the time spent at the arrival locations between each leg (in hours). Percentage station users: A value between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%) that tells us which percentage of users use fast charging stations. This factor is a placeholder and is currently not in use. Start probabilities: A list of values between 0 and 1 (0%-100%) adding up to 1/100% that tells us what the probability of starting the trip is at a given hour. Note that the hours start at day start hour , not at midnight. Repeated sequence: A list of repeated legs (which should follow each other) that form a repeated sequence. Repetition amounts: How often the repeated sequence is repeated. This is a list, with one value per leg repetition (the nth element corresponds to the nth appearance of the sequence in the leg list). Time between repetitions: The time between repetitions of each repeated sequence (in hours). This is a list, with one value per leg repetition (the nth element corresponds to the nth appearance of the sequence in the leg list). Mobility matrix The main aim of the trip initialization/declaration is to create a mobility matrix for the trip. This mobility matrix has, for all combinations of possible start and end locations (i.e. locations connected by a leg in the trip) and for each hour in day number (starting at the day start hour ), the following quantities: 1. Duration: The duration (in hours) of a leg between the start location and the end location. 2. Distance: The distance (in kilometers) of a leg between the start location. 3. Weighted distance: The weighted distance (in kilometers) of a leg between the start location and the end location. This corresponds to using different road types , with given weights and given mixes to account for the fact that vehicles consume more on some road types. 4. Departures amount : The chance that a vehicle, in a given hour, leaves the start location, going to the end location (amount and chance are equivalent here, as we compute on an individual vehicle basis). 5. Departures kilometers: The kilometers driven by vehicles leaving the start location at a given hour and going to the end location. This is given by the departures amount times the distance. 6. Departures weighted kilometers: The weighted (by road type) kilometers driven by vehicles leaving the start location at a given hour and going to the end location. This is given by the departures amount times the weighted distance. 7. Arrivals amount : The chance that a vehicle, in a given hour, arrives to the end location, having started the start location (amount and chance are equivalent here, as we compute on an individual vehicle basis). 8. Arrivals kilometers: The kilometers driven by vehicles arriving to the end location at a given hour, having started at the start location. This is given by the arrivals amount times the distance. 9. Arrivals weighted kilometers: The weighted (by road type) kilometers driven by vehicles arriving to the end location at a given hour, having started at the start location. This is given by the arrivals amount times the weighted distance. The model also produces a version of this mobility matrix for the whole run (which is essentially a copy of the above matrix). This run mobility matrix is the mobility matrix if the trip had a probability of 1 for the whole run. Leg repetitions Is repeat of leg or two legs???? [0, 5, 5, 0] If next leg is also repeated/still has repeats left, then it is repeated after the leg in question so when putting a leg, check if it is repeated. If so, check if the next is repeated, until you have no repeats (or end the list). Add on of each repeated legs then number of repeats goes down by one and redo Have one trip per day type for non-cars Reference to day start hour cross-links with scenario

docs.text: Purpose The purpose of the ChaProEV.toml file is to set parameters that are common for all your scenarios. This page describes the various parameters. You can use the navigation bar on the left to go directly to a group of parameters (or a given parameter). This mostly contains general parameters that should not change too much from case to case. As such, you can take the version provided in the repository (and possibly modify one or two things). variants The variants section of the configuration file sets parameters to create scenario variants (see that page for details). use_variants Setting the use_variants parameters to true creates variants, while setting it to false skips variant creation althogether. csv_version Setting the csv_version to true parameters makes you use csv files to define your variants (in a folder within the variants folder: this folder needs to have the same name as your case). Setting it to false makes you use a toml file in the variants folder (case_name.toml). use_years_in_profiles This is used to create different variants per year when doing car home own driveway and street parking splits parallel_processing This parallel processing section of the configuration file sets parameters to manage the parallel processing/multiprocessing of the model (which reduces the model run time, see link for details). set_amount_of_processes Set this as false if you want the amount of parallel processes to be determined by the model (via the multiprocessing standard library of Python ). Set this to true if you want to set the amount of processes yourself. amount_for_scenarios If you put true in set_amount_of_processes, provide a number of parallel processes here to run scenarios in parallel. amount_for_pickle_saves If you put true in set_amount_of_processes, provide a number of parallel processes here to save the pickle output saves to other formats in parallel (see writing module for details). interim_files This concerns parameters for saving intermediary results to files. pickle Set this to true to save interim results to pickle files. Set this to false not to do this. consumption_tables_frequencies Provide a list of consumption tables frequencies (see consumption module ). The default is the following list ['hourly', 'daily', 'weekly', 'monthly', 'yearly'] save_consumption_table Provide a list of booleans (true or false) to save a given frequency to file (this list needs to have the same length as the above list): true save a file for that frequency and false does not. profile_dataframe These are the headers that appear in output dataframes. headers This one is for profiles (at one-vehicle scale). fleet_headers This one is for the fleet-level dataframes. do_fleet_tables Set this to true to create fleet-level tables. fleet_file_name The file name (has to be a csv inside the input/your_case folder) containing the fleet characteristics. See here for details about this file. sessions_dataframe This is to create the session dataframes. properties Those are the quantities we want to put in the session dataframes. dataframe_headers Those are the headers of the session dataframes at the day level. run_dataframe_headers Those are the headers of the session dataframes for the whole run. display_dataframe_headers These are the headers of the display/final output dataframe headers at vehicle level. display_dataframe_index These give the index of the display/final output dataframe headers. fleet_display_dataframe_headers These are the headers of the display/final output dataframe headers at fleet level. plots This contains parameters for output plots (colors, styles, sizes, etc.). vehicle_temperature_efficiency This set of parameters is for the range-temperature plot. style This is a string with one of the available Matplotlib styles . source_data_folder Folder where the data to plot is. source_data_file File containg the data to plot. fit_color The color name of fit line. fit_line_size The size of the fir line. geotab_data_color The color of the data points. geotab_data_size The size of the data points. title_size The size of the plot title. files General file parameters. input_root The name of the folder where your input data goes (it goes to a subfolder of this with the name of your case). output_root The name of the folder where your output data goes (it goes to a subfolder of this with the name of your case). groupfile_root This is for files that group data (such as (sqlite) databases or Excel workbooks) and will be the name of that grouping file. figures Parameters for plots/figures. dpi Change this to change the resolution of the output figures. outputs Indicate if you want to save your (Matplotlib) figures (true if you do, false if you don't) in various formats. dataframe_outputs Indicate if you want to save your Pandas DataFrames in the listed formats (put a true if you want to do so, false if you don't). Clipboard saves to the local clipboard, not a file. maps Parameters for making maps. map_data_folder The folder where the map data is. area_data_file_name The file containing map areas. general_exclusion_codes Excluded map codes. border_data_file_prefix The prefix of the border data file. border_data_file_suffix The suffix of the border data file. points_data_file_prefix The prefix of the points data file. points_data_file_suffix The suffix of the points data file. country_code_header The header we use for country codes. country_code_header_in_map_data The country code header in tnhe source data. heat_bar_map The heat bar map/scale we want to use for maps (is the name of a color bar ). colors Definitions of custom colors (with RGB values, from 0 to 255). color_bars You can deine color bars here, by listing the colors they use (in order). unit_conversions This contains various constants used for unit conversions, such as the amount of Joules in a kiloWatt-hour. Some are grouped (time conversions). The times subpart also contains the codes for weekend day numbers and the index of the first hour in the year (often 0, but sometimes 1, as for the SPINE toolbox). numbers This contains a threshold to avoid issues with float precision and exteremely small values that are actually zero. consumption This contains settings (mostly headers and display names) related to the connusmption tables. energy_carriers A list of the energy carriers that come in the consumption table. consumption_table_name The name of the consumption table. time_header The header used for the time index in the consumption table. distance_header The header used for the distance column in the consumption table. fleet_distance_header The header used for the distance column in the fleet consumption table. energy_carriers_consumption_names The headers for each emergy carrier in the consumption table. fleet_energy_carriers_consumption_names The headers for each emergy carrier in the fleet consumption table. home_type These are parametrers related to the home type split (split for cars between cars with their own driveway and street parking). do_car_home_type_split Set this to true to compute the split. Set it to false not to do it. percentages_file The file name (has to be a csv inside the input/your_case folder) containing the spli. See here for details about this file. index_name The index header in the source file. own_driveway_name The header for the own driveway percentage. Also used for the output profile file names. on_street_name The header for the street parking percentage. Used for the output profile file names. profiles_index The index for the profile outputs. sessions_index The index for the sessions outputs. sessions_values_columns The columns of the sessions dataframes. sessions Parameters used for the sessions . produce Set to true if you want to create sessions , to false if you don't. generate_profiles Set to true if you want to [generate profiles from sessions][scenarios_module.md#Generate-profiles-from-sessions], to false if you don't. standard_profiles produce Set to true if you want to produce standard charging profiles , false if you don't. progress_bars Parameters related to displaying progress bars. display_scenario_run Set to true to show a progress bar for the computing of scenarios, false if you don't. scenario_run_description Text to display for the scenarios progress bar. display_saving_pool_run Set to true to show a progress bar for the saving of output files, false if you don't. saving_pool_run_description Text to display for the output file saving progress bar. discharge Parameters related to vehicle discharge. no_discharge_efficiency_output Message to display if the discharge efficiencncy value is empty. no_charge_efficiency_output Message to display if the charge efficiencncy value is empty.

docs.text: Purpose The purpose of the ChaProEV.toml file is to set parameters that are common for all your scenarios. This page describes the various parameters. You can use the navigation bar on the left to go directly to a group of parameters (or a given parameter). variants The variants section of the configuration file sets parameters to create scenario variants (see that page for details). use_variants Setting the use_variants parameters to true creates variants, while setting it to false skips variant creation althogether. csv_version Setting the csv_version to true parameters makes you use csv files to define your variants (in a folder within the variants folder: this folder needs to have the same name as your case). Setting it to false makes you use a toml file in the variants folder (case_name.toml). use_years_in_profiles This is used to create different variants per year when doing car home own driveway and street parking splits parallel_processing This parallel processing section of the configuration file sets parameters to manage the parallel processing/multiprocessing of the model (which reduces the model run time, see link for details). set_amount_of_processes Set this as false if you want the amount of parallel processes to be determined by the model (via the multiprocessing standard library of Python ). docs.text: Residential grid congestion Goal We want to model the impact of residential grid connection issues on charging profiles charging demand can be high a the same time as other demand is high, so chargign session demands might be delayed, reduced or outrighht denied This will impact they way vehicles charge and change the charging . We look at residential neighbourhood because it is likely that such conflicts will occur (simultaeous demand, also the fact that in other locations the grid might besolely dedicated to EV charging). When to use The parameters include_residential_grid_congestion (set to either true or false ) in the [grid] section of your scenario tells if you are using this modelling or not. Set it to true if you want to add residetial grid congestion issues to our profile. If you don't want to include such effects, or if you want to investigate them in another model (fr example an optimisation one) using the profiles provided by ChaProEV, or if it is not relevant (e.g. vehicles such as busses that charge in dedidcated locations) This is mostly meant for cars. Approach Scope One transformer for the neighbourhood with a given capacity and a certain amount of lines, ach having its own capacity (sum of lines capacity is transformer capacity) This provides two constraints. One at transformer level, and one at each level so issues could come at the whole neighbourhood level, as well as at a more local level (e.g. a street has many EVs and their users charge at the same time as they have elecxtricity demand for other purposes) Power line capacities The model distributes the transformer capacity over its connected power lines. For each power line, a relative capacity weight is drawn from a bounded beta distribution . These weights are subsequently normalised and multiplied by the transformer capacity. This introduces variation between the capacities assigned to individual power lines while ensuring that the sum of all line capacities remains equal to the transformer capacity: \[ P_{\mathrm{line},i} = P_{\mathrm{transformer}} \frac{w_i}{\sum_j w_j} \] and therefore: \[ \sum_i P_{\mathrm{line},i} = P_{\mathrm{transformer}} \] This represents a deliberately conservative modelling assumption. The available transformer capacity is effectively divided between the individual power lines, and the model subsequently tests the power demand on each line against its assigned capacity. Because the line capacities sum to the transformer capacity, satisfying the capacity restriction of every individual line also guarantees that the total transformer-capacity restriction is satisfied. In an actual distribution grid, the physical capacities of the outgoing power lines do not necessarily sum to the transformer capacity and may collectively exceed it. If one line is lightly loaded, another line may therefore carry a larger share of the transformer load, provided that its own physical capacity and the total transformer capacity are not exceeded. The model does not currently represent such dynamic sharing of transformer capacity between lines. Instead, each line receives a fixed share of the transformer capacity. This results in a conservative representation of the line-level capacity restrictions. Assigning EV users to lines To determine whether the individual power lines can support the EV charging demand connected to them, the model needs to know which EV users are connected to each line. This is done in two steps. First, the EV chargers are assigned to power lines. The users associated with each charger are then assigned to the same line. Chargers are assigned while respecting the capacity of each power line. A charger can only be assigned to a line if the remaining line capacity is at least equal to the rated power of the charger. The sum of the rated powers of all chargers assigned to a line can therefore never exceed that line's capacity. The chargers are processed from highest to lowest rated power. Assigning the largest chargers first reduces the risk of filling the lines with smaller chargers in such a way that insufficient capacity remains for a larger charger, even though a feasible allocation could otherwise have existed. For each charger, the model determines which lines have sufficient remaining capacity. The charger is then randomly assigned to one of these eligible lines, with the probability of selecting a line proportional to its remaining capacity: \[ p_i = \frac{P_{\mathrm{remaining},i}} {\sum_{j \in E} P_{\mathrm{remaining},j}} \] where \(E\) is the set of lines with sufficient remaining capacity for the charger. After assigning a charger, its rated power is subtracted from the remaining capacity of the selected line. Consequently, lines with more available capacity are more likely to receive chargers, while lines that are becoming more heavily occupied become progressively less likely to receive additional chargers. This procedure allows both situations in which some lines have no EV chargers and situations in which multiple chargers are connected to the same line. If no line has sufficient remaining capacity for a charger, the assignment fails. The method is a greedy stochastic allocation: processing the largest chargers first reduces the chance of an unsuccessful allocation, but does not mathematically guarantee finding a feasible allocation whenever one exists. Finally, the model looks up the EV users associated with each charger and assigns these users to the same power line as their charger. This provides the mapping between EV users and power lines that is subsequently used to aggregate their charging profiles and test the line-level capacity restrictions. Note: The sum of the nominal powers of all chargers cannot exceed the transformer capacity. This is a conservative modelling assumption that ensures that all chargers connected to the transformer could operate simultaneously at their nominal power without exceeding the transformer capacity. If the total charger power exceeds the transformer capacity, the model cannot assign all chargers within the available capacity. The following model inputs can be adjusted: Increase the transformer capacity. Reduce the nominal power of the chargers. Increase the proportion of street chargers. Street chargers are shared between users, reducing the number of chargers required. Reduce the street charger connectivity. More users then share each street charger, also reducing the number of chargers required. Assignment of home chargers and connectivity Home chargers are created after the users have been generated. The procedure distinguishes between users with their own driveway and users who park on the street. A user with an own driveway receives an individual home charger and therefore has a home connectivity of 1. Whenever the vehicle is at home, the home charger is available to that user. For street parking, chargers are shared between multiple users. The configured street-parking connectivity is used to determine the number of chargers that should be available. For \(N\) street-parking users with a configured connectivity \(c\) , the expected number of chargers is $$ N_{\mathrm{chargers, expected}} = N_{\mathrm{users}} \times c. $$ Because the model must create a discrete number of physical chargers, this value is rounded to the nearest integer, with half values rounded upwards. If there are street-parking users, at least one charger is created. A connectivity of zero is therefore not allowed when street-parking users are present. For example, with 12 street-parking users and a configured connectivity of 0.25: \[ 12 \times 0.25 = 3 \] and three street chargers are created. The street-parking users are first randomly shuffled and are subsequently assigned to the available chargers in round-robin order. This makes the assignment stochastic while distributing the users as evenly as possible over the chargers: the numbers of users assigned to any two chargers can differ by at most one. After the users have been assigned, their actual home connectivity is recalculated from the number of users sharing their charger: \[ c_{\mathrm{user}} = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{users\ on\ charger}}}. \] For example, a charger shared by four users gives each of those users a connectivity of 0.25, while a charger shared by three users gives each user a connectivity of approximately 0.333. The recalculation is necessary because the configured connectivity represents the desired average availability, whereas the model contains a finite number of users and a discrete number of chargers. The exact configured connectivity can therefore not always be reproduced. For example, if 11 street-parking users have a configured connectivity of 0.25, the expected number of chargers is \[ 11 \times 0.25 = 2.75, \] which results in three physical chargers. The users are then distributed as 4, 4 and 3 users over these chargers, giving individual connectivities of 0.25, 0.25 and approximately 0.333, respectively. This preserves the physical interpretation of connectivity: it represents the probability that the shared charger assigned to a user is available when that user wants to charge. The updated connectivity is stored on the user's home Location . The charging DataFrame is deliberately created only after the local grid and charger assignment have been constructed. This ensures that the stochastic charging-session availability draws use the final connectivity resulting from the actual charger allocation, rather than the original scenario-level connectivity. Non-EV demand Household node demand profiles To determine the electricity demand on each power line, the model first creates an individual fixed non-EV electricity profile for every household node. This profile represents the net electricity exchange between the household node and the grid at each time step before EV charging and stationary-battery operation are taken into account. Each household node can contain three components that contribute directly to this initial non-EV profile: Basic household electricity demand Heat-pump electricity demand Solar-panel production Demand from the household and heat pump is represented as positive power, whereas electricity production from the solar panels is represented as negative power. The initial net non-EV profile of a household node is therefore calculated as: \[ P_{\mathrm{non\text{-}EV},n}(t) = P_{\mathrm{household},n}(t) + P_{\mathrm{heat\ pump},n}(t) + P_{\mathrm{solar},n}(t) \] A positive value indicates that the household node has a net electricity demand from the grid at that time step, while a negative value indicates that the household node is supplying electricity to the grid. A household node can additionally contain a stationary battery. However, the stationary-battery power profile cannot yet be determined when the household node is created. Battery charging and discharging depend on the complete power situation, including EV charging. The battery is therefore initially represented by its capacity, charging-power limit, and discharging-power limit, while its power profile and charge level are initialised at zero. The model creates the basic household demand, heat pump, solar panels, and stationary battery separately for each household node. Their stochastic properties are therefore determined at the individual household level. Only the basic household, heat-pump, and solar-panel profiles are combined at this stage to obtain the initial net non-EV profile. These node-level profiles are subsequently assigned to the power lines based on the number of household nodes allocated to each line. The profiles of the nodes connected to a line are summed to obtain the line-level non-EV demand profile. At the same time, the stationary batteries belonging to these nodes are added to the stationary-battery capacity available on the corresponding power line. Basic household electricity demand The basic household electricity demand represents electricity consumption excluding EV charging, heat pumps, and home batteries. These components are modelled separately and are subsequently combined to obtain the complete net non-EV profile of each household node. For each household, the model first draws the total basic electricity demand for the simulation period from a bounded beta distribution. The minimum, typical, and maximum demand are provided as model inputs. This allows individual households to have different total electricity demands while keeping these within the specified bounds. The temporal distribution of this electricity demand is determined using a set of demand-profile shapes provided as model input. One of these shapes is randomly selected for each household, with user-defined probabilities determining how frequently the different shapes are selected. The temporal resolution of the selected demand shape does not necessarily have to equal the temporal resolution of the simulation. If the demand shape has a lower temporal resolution, its values are repeated to obtain the required model resolution. For example, a 15-minute profile can be converted to a 1-minute profile by repeating each value 15 times. If the demand shape has a higher temporal resolution, consecutive values are averaged. The two resolutions must have an integer ratio; otherwise, the model raises an error. After any required resolution conversion, the demand shape is normalised: \[ \sum_t s(t) = 1 \] where \(s(t)\) is the normalised household demand shape. It is then scaled using the total electricity demand drawn for that household and converted from energy per time step to average power in kW: \[ P_{\mathrm{household}}(t) = \frac{ E_{\mathrm{household,run}} \, s(t) }{ \Delta t } \] where \(E_{\mathrm{household,run}}\) is the total basic household electricity demand over the simulation period in kWh and \(\Delta t\) is the model time-step duration in hours. This ensures that integrating the resulting power profile over the complete simulation period reproduces the drawn household electricity demand: \[ \sum_t P_{\mathrm{household}}(t)\Delta t = E_{\mathrm{household,run}} \] The resulting profile represents the basic household electricity demand in kW at every model time step and is subsequently combined with the heat-pump and solar-panel profiles to obtain the household node's initial net non-EV power profile. Stationary-battery operation is determined separately at a later stage, once the complete power demand, including EV charging, is known. Heat-pump demand Heat pumps are included as an additional source of household electricity demand. Whether a household has a heat pump is determined stochastically using a user-defined heat-pump adoption rate. For households with a heat pump, the total heat demand over the simulation period is drawn from a bounded beta distribution. The minimum, typical, and maximum heat demands are provided as model inputs. The resulting demand represents useful thermal energy and is therefore expressed in kWh of heat. The coefficient of performance (COP) of the heat pump is also drawn from a bounded beta distribution. The COP describes the ratio between the useful heat delivered by the heat pump and its electricity consumption. The total electricity consumption required to provide the drawn heat demand is therefore: \[ E_{\mathrm{HP,run}} = \frac{ Q_{\mathrm{heat,run}} }{ COP } \] where \(Q_{\mathrm{heat,run}}\) is the total heat demand during the simulation period and \(E_{\mathrm{HP,run}}\) is the corresponding heat-pump electricity demand. The temporal distribution of the heat demand is determined using a set of heat-demand profile shapes provided as model input. One profile is randomly selected for each household with a heat pump using user-defined probabilities. The selected profile is resized to match the simulation period and temporal resolution, if necessary, and normalised so that its values sum to one. The heat-pump electricity-demand profile is then calculated as: \[ P_{\mathrm{HP}}(t) = \frac{ Q_{\mathrm{heat,run}} \, s_{\mathrm{heat}}(t) }{ COP \, \Delta t } \] where \(s_{\mathrm{heat}}(t)\) is the normalised heat-demand shape and \(\Delta t\) is the model time-step duration in hours. The resulting profile therefore represents the average electrical power demand of the heat pump in kW at every model time step. The electricity consumed by the heat pump is also included in the household electricity-demand reference used to determine solar-panel production. The reference demand for sizing solar production therefore consists of the basic household electricity demand plus the heat pump's electrical energy demand: \[ E_{\mathrm{reference}} = E_{\mathrm{household,run}} + \frac{ Q_{\mathrm{heat,run}} }{ COP } \] For households without a heat pump, both the heat demand and heat-pump electricity-demand profile are zero. Solar-panel production Solar panels are included in the household node as a source of electricity production. Whether a household has solar panels is determined stochastically using a user-defined solar-panel adoption rate. Each household therefore has a probability of receiving solar panels equal to the specified adoption rate. For households with solar panels, the total solar production over the simulation period is determined relative to the household electricity demand, including heat-pump electricity demand if a heat pump is present: \[ E_{\mathrm{reference}} = E_{\mathrm{household,run}} + \frac{ Q_{\mathrm{heat,run}} }{ COP } \] The total solar production is then: \[ E_{\mathrm{solar,run}} = E_{\mathrm{reference}} r_{\mathrm{solar}} \] where \(E_{\mathrm{reference}}\) is the household electricity-demand reference over the simulation period and \(r_{\mathrm{solar}}\) is the assumed ratio between solar production and household electricity demand. The model allows this ratio to depend on whether the household also has a home battery. Separate solar-production-to-demand ratios can therefore be provided for households with and without a home battery. This makes it possible to represent a relationship between home-battery ownership and the amount of installed solar generation. The temporal distribution of solar production is determined using a set of solar-production profile shapes provided as model input. One profile variant is randomly selected for each household with solar panels, using user-defined probabilities for the different variants. The selected profile is resized to match the temporal resolution and length of the simulation, if necessary, using the same profile-reshaping procedure as for the basic household demand. The resulting production shape is normalised: \[ \sum_t s_{\mathrm{solar}}(t) = 1 \] The normalised shape is subsequently scaled to the total solar production over the simulation period. The resulting energy per time step is converted from kWh to average power in kW by dividing it by the model time-step duration in hours: \[ P_{\mathrm{solar}}(t) = - \frac{ E_{\mathrm{solar,run}} s_{\mathrm{solar}}(t) }{ \Delta t } \] where \(\Delta t\) is the model time-step duration in hours. Solar production is represented as negative power because the grid convention used in the model considers electricity consumption to be positive and electricity production to be negative. Consequently: \[ -\sum_t P_{\mathrm{solar}}(t)\Delta t = E_{\mathrm{solar,run}} \] For households without solar panels, both solar production and the corresponding power profile are zero. The solar-production profile is subsequently combined with the basic household and heat-pump demand profiles to obtain the household node's initial net non-EV power profile. Stationary batteries Stationary batteries can be present both at household nodes and in combination with EV chargers. Unlike basic household demand, heat-pump demand, and solar production, a stationary battery does not receive a fixed power profile when the residential grid is initialised. Its charging and discharging behaviour depends on the complete power situation, including EV charging, and can therefore only be determined at a later stage. During grid initialisation, the model consequently determines the battery's energy capacity in kWh and its maximum charging and discharging powers in kW. Its charge-level and power-profile series are initially set to zero. Household stationary batteries Whether a household has a stationary battery is determined stochastically. Different adoption rates can be specified for households with and without solar panels. For a household that receives a stationary battery, its capacity is based on the household's average daily electricity demand and solar production during the simulation period. Three separate contributions are considered: basic household electricity demand; heat-pump electricity demand; solar-panel production. The duration of the simulation period in days is: \[ D_{\mathrm{run}} = \frac{ N_{\mathrm{steps}} \Delta t }{ 24 } \] where \(N_{\mathrm{steps}}\) is the number of model time steps and \(\Delta t\) is the time-step duration in hours. The capacity associated with basic household demand is: \[ C_{\mathrm{basic}} = \frac{ E_{\mathrm{household,run}} }{ D_{\mathrm{run}} } d_{\mathrm{basic}} \] where \(d_{\mathrm{basic}}\) is the configured number of reserve days for basic household demand. For heat-pump demand, the thermal energy demand is first converted to electrical energy using the heat pump's COP: \[ C_{\mathrm{HP}} = \frac{ Q_{\mathrm{heat,run}} / COP }{ D_{\mathrm{run}} } d_{\mathrm{HP}} \] where \(d_{\mathrm{HP}}\) is the configured number of reserve days for heat-pump electricity demand. The solar-production contribution is: \[ C_{\mathrm{solar}} = \frac{ E_{\mathrm{solar,run}} }{ D_{\mathrm{run}} } d_{\mathrm{solar}} \] where \(d_{\mathrm{solar}}\) is the configured number of reserve days associated with solar production. The total stationary-battery capacity of the household is then: \[ C_{\mathrm{battery}} = C_{\mathrm{basic}} + C_{\mathrm{HP}} + C_{\mathrm{solar}} \] The maximum charging and discharging powers of household stationary batteries are specified directly by the grid parameters. Stationary batteries associated with EV chargers EV chargers can also receive a stationary battery. Whether this occurs is determined stochastically using the configured adoption rate for stationary batteries associated with EV chargers. The capacity of such a battery is based on the rated EV-charging power and a configured number of reserve hours: \[ C_{\mathrm{charger\ battery}} = P_{\mathrm{charger}} t_{\mathrm{reserve}} \] This means that a fully charged stationary battery contains enough energy to provide the charger's rated charging power for the configured reserve duration, or a lower power for a correspondingly longer duration. The stationary battery's maximum discharging power is equal to the charger's EV-charging power: \[ P_{\mathrm{battery,discharge,max}} = P_{\mathrm{charger,charge}} \] The stationary battery's maximum charging power is equal to the charger's reverse-power capability: \[ P_{\mathrm{battery,charge,max}} = P_{\mathrm{charger,reverse}} \] The latter represents the reverse power direction through the charger. Aggregation of stationary batteries on power lines Stationary batteries are ultimately represented at power-line level. Batteries associated with EV chargers are assigned directly to the line containing the corresponding charger. Household stationary batteries are assigned to the line to which their household node is allocated. For all stationary batteries connected to a line, their capacities and power limits are added: \[ C_{\mathrm{battery,line},i} = \sum_{b \in B_i} C_b \] \[ P_{\mathrm{charge,max},i} = \sum_{b \in B_i} P_{\mathrm{charge,max},b} \] \[ P_{\mathrm{discharge,max},i} = \sum_{b \in B_i} P_{\mathrm{discharge,max},b} \] where \(B_i\) is the set of stationary batteries assigned to line \(i\) . The charge-level and battery-power series are aggregated in the same way. Because no battery dispatch has yet taken place during grid initialisation, these series initially contain zeros. The resulting line-level stationary battery therefore represents the combined stationary-battery capacity and power capability connected to that power line. Its actual charge level and power profile are determined later, when the complete line load, including EV charging, is known. Modelling assumption: The batteries connected to a power line are treated as a single aggregated stationary battery at line level. Their capacities, charging powers, discharging powers, charge levels, and power profiles are added together. This means that the model does not preserve constraints associated with the distribution of stored energy between the individual physical batteries once they have been aggregated. Assigning household nodes to lines The household nodes are distributed over the power lines proportionally to their capacities. For each line, the ideal number of household nodes is first calculated from its share of the total line capacity: \[ n_i^* = N_{\mathrm{households}} \frac{P_{\mathrm{line},i}} {\sum_j P_{\mathrm{line},j}} \] Since the number of household nodes assigned to a line must be an integer, these ideal values cannot generally be used directly. The model therefore applies the largest remainder method . First, the ideal number of nodes for each line is rounded down to the nearest integer. This generally leaves a small number of household nodes unassigned. These remaining nodes are assigned, one by one, to the lines with the largest fractional remainders in their ideal allocations. This ensures that the total number of assigned nodes is exactly equal to the number of households, while keeping the distribution as close as possible to proportional to the line capacities. A line may receive no household nodes if the number of households is small relative to the number of lines or its proportional allocation is sufficiently small. Assigning non-EV demand to lines After determining the number of household nodes connected to each power line, the corresponding non-EV demand profiles are assigned to these lines. The household profiles have already been generated using random draws, so no additional randomisation is applied during this assignment. Instead, the profiles are assigned sequentially according to the previously determined number of nodes per line. For each power line, the non-EV demand profiles of all household nodes assigned to that line are summed to obtain a single line-level non-EV demand profile: \[ P_{\mathrm{non\text{-}EV},i}(t) = \sum_{n \in N_i} P_{\mathrm{non\text{-}EV},n}(t) \] where \(N_i\) is the set of household nodes assigned to line \(i\) . The resulting profile represents the initial non-EV household demand connected to that power line at each time step, before stationary-battery operation is included. At the same time, the stationary batteries belonging to the assigned household nodes are added to the stationary-battery object of the corresponding power line. Their capacities, charging-power limits, discharging-power limits, charge levels, and power profiles are summed. Any stationary batteries associated with EV chargers have already been assigned to their chargers' respective power lines. The resulting power line therefore contains both an initial fixed non-EV power profile and an aggregated stationary battery. The battery power profile is initially zero and is determined later together with EV charging. The eventual power on a line can therefore be represented conceptually as: \[ P_{\mathrm{line},i}(t) = P_{\mathrm{non\text{-}EV},i}(t) + P_{\mathrm{EV},i}(t) + P_{\mathrm{battery},i}(t) \] using the model convention that electricity demand is positive and electricity supply is negative. Battery charging therefore contributes positive power, whereas battery discharging contributes negative power. The order of the probabilities must correspond to the order in profile_variants . Solar-panel adoption rate adoption_rate_solar_panels specifies the probability that a household has solar panels. Production-to-demand ratio without stationary battery run_production_as_proportion_of_demand_if_no_battery specifies total solar production over the simulation period as a proportion of household electricity demand for households without a stationary battery. Household electricity demand includes heat-pump electricity demand when a heat pump is present. For example, a value of 1.0 means that total solar production over the simulation period is equal to the household electricity-demand reference used for solar production. Using a separate value for households with stationary batteries makes it possible to represent a relationship between stationary-battery adoption and installed solar generation. The names must correspond to columns in the solar profile-shape source file. Solar profile proportions profile_proportions specifies the probabilities with which the corresponding solar-production profile variants are selected. The order of these probabilities must correspond to the order in profile_variants . Solar profile-shape source profile_shapes_source specifies the path to the CSV file containing the available solar-production profile shapes. Adoption rate for EV-charger batteries adoption_rate_for_EV_chargers specifies the probability that an EV charger has an associated stationary battery. EV-charger battery reserve hours EV_reserve_hours specifies the number of hours for which a fully charged stationary battery associated with an EV charger should be able to provide the rated charging power of that charger. Its battery capacity is therefore calculated as: \[ C_{\mathrm{battery}} = P_{\mathrm{charger}} t_{\mathrm{reserve}} \] For example, a 7.4 kW charger with EV_reserve_hours = 2.0 results in a stationary-battery capacity of 14.8 kWh. The battery's maximum discharge power is equal to the charger's charging power, while its maximum charging power is equal to the charger's reverse-power capability. Household battery adoption rate without solar panels adoption_rate_home_batteries_if_not_solar_panels specifies the probability that a household without solar panels has a stationary battery. Separate adoption rates make it possible to represent the relationship between solar-panel ownership and stationary-battery ownership. Charging power charging_power_kW specifies the maximum charging power in kW of a household stationary battery. This parameter applies to household stationary batteries. The charging power of a stationary battery associated with an EV charger is instead derived from the reverse-power capability of that charger. Discharging power discharging_power_kW specifies the maximum discharging power in kW of a household stationary battery. This parameter applies to household stationary batteries. The discharging power of a stationary battery associated with an EV charger is instead derived from the rated charging power of that charger. Reserve days for basic household demand reserve_days_basic determines the contribution of basic household electricity demand to stationary-battery capacity. The model first calculates the household's average daily basic electricity demand over the simulation period. This is multiplied by reserve_days_basic to determine the corresponding contribution to battery capacity. Reserve days for heat-pump demand reserve_days_heat_pump determines the contribution of heat-pump electricity demand to stationary-battery capacity. The total heat demand is first divided by the heat pump's COP to obtain electricity demand. The average daily heat-pump electricity demand is then multiplied by reserve_days_heat_pump . Reserve days for solar production reserve_days_solar_panels determines the contribution of solar production to stationary-battery capacity. The model calculates the average daily solar production over the simulation period and multiplies this value by reserve_days_solar_panels . The complete capacity of a household stationary battery is the sum of the capacity contributions from basic household demand, heat-pump electricity demand, and solar-panel production.
