docs.text: One transformer for the neighbourhood with a given capacity and a certain amount of lines, ach having its own capacity (sum of lines capacity is transformer capacity) This provides two constraints. One at transformer level, and one at each level so issues could come at the whole neighbourhood level, as well as at a more local level (e.g. a street has many EVs and their users charge at the same time as they have elecxtricity demand for other purposes)
docs.title: Scope

docs.text: The model distributes the transformer capacity over its connected power lines. For each power line, a relative capacity weight is drawn from a bounded beta distribution . These weights are subsequently normalised and multiplied by the transformer capacity. This introduces variation between the capacities assigned to individual power lines while ensuring that the sum of all line capacities remains equal to the transformer capacity: \[ P_{\mathrm{line},i} = P_{\mathrm{transformer}} \frac{w_i}{\sum_j w_j} \] and therefore: \[ \sum_i P_{\mathrm{line},i} = P_{\mathrm{transformer}} \] This represents a deliberately conservative modelling assumption. The available transformer capacity is effectively divided between the individual power lines, and the model subsequently tests the power demand on each line against its assigned capacity. Because the line capacities sum to the transformer capacity, satisfying the capacity restriction of every individual line also guarantees that the total transformer-capacity restriction is satisfied. In an actual distribution grid, the physical capacities of the outgoing power lines do not necessarily sum to the transformer capacity and may collectively exceed it. If one line is lightly loaded, another line may therefore carry a larger share of the transformer load, provided that its own physical capacity and the total transformer capacity are not exceeded. The model does not currently represent such dynamic sharing of transformer capacity between lines. Instead, each line receives a fixed share of the transformer capacity. This results in a conservative representation of the line-level capacity restrictions.
docs.title: Power line capacities

docs.text: To determine whether the individual power lines can support the EV charging demand connected to them, the model needs to know which EV users are connected to each line. This is done in two steps. First, the EV chargers are assigned to power lines. The users associated with each charger are then assigned to the same line. Chargers are assigned while respecting the capacity of each power line. A charger can only be assigned to a line if the remaining line capacity is at least equal to the rated power of the charger. The sum of the rated powers of all chargers assigned to a line can therefore never exceed that line's capacity. The chargers are processed from highest to lowest rated power. Assigning the largest chargers first reduces the risk of filling the lines with smaller chargers in such a way that insufficient capacity remains for a larger charger, even though a feasible allocation could otherwise have existed. For each charger, the model determines which lines have sufficient remaining capacity. The charger is then randomly assigned to one of these eligible lines, with the probability of selecting a line proportional to its remaining capacity: \[ p_i = \frac{P_{\mathrm{remaining},i}} {\sum_{j \in E} P_{\mathrm{remaining},j}} \] where \(E\) is the set of lines with sufficient remaining capacity for the charger. After assigning a charger, its rated power is subtracted from the remaining capacity of the selected line. Consequently, lines with more available capacity are more likely to receive chargers, while lines that are becoming more heavily occupied become progressively less likely to receive additional chargers. This procedure allows both situations in which some lines have no EV chargers and situations in which multiple chargers are connected to the same line. If no line has sufficient remaining capacity for a charger, the assignment fails. The method is a greedy stochastic allocation: processing the largest chargers first reduces the chance of an unsuccessful allocation, but does not mathematically guarantee finding a feasible allocation whenever one exists. Finally, the model looks up the EV users associated with each charger and assigns these users to the same power line as their charger. This provides the mapping between EV users and power lines that is subsequently used to aggregate their charging profiles and test the line-level capacity restrictions. Note: The sum of the nominal powers of all chargers cannot exceed the transformer capacity. This is a conservative modelling assumption that ensures that all chargers connected to the transformer could operate simultaneously at their nominal power without exceeding the transformer capacity. If the total charger power exceeds the transformer capacity, the model cannot assign all chargers within the available capacity. The following model inputs can be adjusted: Increase the transformer capacity. Reduce the nominal power of the chargers. Increase the proportion of street chargers. Street chargers are shared between users, reducing the number of chargers required. Reduce the street charger connectivity. More users then share each street charger, also reducing the number of chargers required.
docs.title: Assigning EV users to lines

docs.text: Home chargers are created after the users have been generated. The procedure distinguishes between users with their own driveway and users who park on the street. A user with an own driveway receives an individual home charger and therefore has a home connectivity of 1. Whenever the vehicle is at home, the home charger is available to that user. For street parking, chargers are shared between multiple users. The configured street-parking connectivity is used to determine the number of chargers that should be available. For \(N\) street-parking users with a configured connectivity \(c\) , the expected number of chargers is $$ N_{\mathrm{chargers, expected}} = N_{\mathrm{users}} \times c. $$ Because the model must create a discrete number of physical chargers, this value is rounded to the nearest integer, with half values rounded upwards. If there are street-parking users, at least one charger is created. A connectivity of zero is therefore not allowed when street-parking users are present. For example, with 12 street-parking users and a configured connectivity of 0.25: \[ 12 \times 0.25 = 3 \] and three street chargers are created. The street-parking users are first randomly shuffled and are subsequently assigned to the available chargers in round-robin order. This makes the assignment stochastic while distributing the users as evenly as possible over the chargers: the numbers of users assigned to any two chargers can differ by at most one. After the users have been assigned, their actual home connectivity is recalculated from the number of users sharing their charger: \[ c_{\mathrm{user}} = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{users\ on\ charger}}}. \] For example, a charger shared by four users gives each of those users a connectivity of 0.25, while a charger shared by three users gives each user a connectivity of approximately 0.333. The recalculation is necessary because the configured connectivity represents the desired average availability, whereas the model contains a finite number of users and a discrete number of chargers. The exact configured connectivity can therefore not always be reproduced. For example, if 11 street-parking users have a configured connectivity of 0.25, the expected number of chargers is \[ 11 \times 0.25 = 2.75, \] which results in three physical chargers. The users are then distributed as 4, 4 and 3 users over these chargers, giving individual connectivities of 0.25, 0.25 and approximately 0.333, respectively. This preserves the physical interpretation of connectivity: it represents the probability that the shared charger assigned to a user is available when that user wants to charge. The updated connectivity is stored on the user's home Location . The charging DataFrame is deliberately created only after the local grid and charger assignment have been constructed. This ensures that the stochastic charging-session availability draws use the final connectivity resulting from the actual charger allocation, rather than the original scenario-level connectivity.
docs.title: Assignment of home chargers and connectivity

docs.text: To determine the electricity demand on each power line, the model first creates an individual fixed non-EV electricity profile for every household node. This profile represents the net electricity exchange between the household node and the grid at each time step before EV charging and stationary-battery operation are taken into account. Each household node can contain three components that contribute directly to this initial non-EV profile: Basic household electricity demand Heat-pump electricity demand Solar-panel production Demand from the household and heat pump is represented as positive power, whereas electricity production from the solar panels is represented as negative power. The initial net non-EV profile of a household node is therefore calculated as: \[ P_{\mathrm{non\text{-}EV},n}(t) = P_{\mathrm{household},n}(t) + P_{\mathrm{heat\ pump},n}(t) + P_{\mathrm{solar},n}(t) \] A positive value indicates that the household node has a net electricity demand from the grid at that time step, while a negative value indicates that the household node is supplying electricity to the grid. A household node can additionally contain a stationary battery. However, the stationary-battery power profile cannot yet be determined when the household node is created. Battery charging and discharging depend on the complete power situation, including EV charging. The battery is therefore initially represented by its capacity, charging-power limit, and discharging-power limit, while its power profile and charge level are initialised at zero. The model creates the basic household demand, heat pump, solar panels, and stationary battery separately for each household node. Their stochastic properties are therefore determined at the individual household level. Only the basic household, heat-pump, and solar-panel profiles are combined at this stage to obtain the initial net non-EV profile. These node-level profiles are subsequently assigned to the power lines based on the number of household nodes allocated to each line. The profiles of the nodes connected to a line are summed to obtain the line-level non-EV demand profile. At the same time, the stationary batteries belonging to these nodes are added to the stationary-battery capacity available on the corresponding power line.
docs.title: Household node demand profiles

docs.text: The basic household electricity demand represents electricity consumption excluding EV charging, heat pumps, and home batteries. These components are modelled separately and are subsequently combined to obtain the complete net non-EV profile of each household node. For each household, the model first draws the total basic electricity demand for the simulation period from a bounded beta distribution. The minimum, typical, and maximum demand are provided as model inputs. This allows individual households to have different total electricity demands while keeping these within the specified bounds. The temporal distribution of this electricity demand is determined using a set of demand-profile shapes provided as model input. One of these shapes is randomly selected for each household, with user-defined probabilities determining how frequently the different shapes are selected. The temporal resolution of the selected demand shape does not necessarily have to equal the temporal resolution of the simulation. If the demand shape has a lower temporal resolution, its values are repeated to obtain the required model resolution. For example, a 15-minute profile can be converted to a 1-minute profile by repeating each value 15 times. If the demand shape has a higher temporal resolution, consecutive values are averaged. The two resolutions must have an integer ratio; otherwise, the model raises an error. After any required resolution conversion, the demand shape is normalised: \[ \sum_t s(t) = 1 \] where \(s(t)\) is the normalised household demand shape. It is then scaled using the total electricity demand drawn for that household and converted from energy per time step to average power in kW: \[ P_{\mathrm{household}}(t) = \frac{ E_{\mathrm{household,run}} \, s(t) }{ \Delta t } \] where \(E_{\mathrm{household,run}}\) is the total basic household electricity demand over the simulation period in kWh and \(\Delta t\) is the model time-step duration in hours. This ensures that integrating the resulting power profile over the complete simulation period reproduces the drawn household electricity demand: \[ \sum_t P_{\mathrm{household}}(t)\Delta t = E_{\mathrm{household,run}} \] The resulting profile represents the basic household electricity demand in kW at every model time step and is subsequently combined with the heat-pump and solar-panel profiles to obtain the household node's initial net non-EV power profile. Stationary-battery operation is determined separately at a later stage, once the complete power demand, including EV charging, is known.
docs.title: Basic household electricity demand

docs.text: Heat pumps are included as an additional source of household electricity demand. Whether a household has a heat pump is determined stochastically using a user-defined heat-pump adoption rate. For households with a heat pump, the total heat demand over the simulation period is drawn from a bounded beta distribution. The minimum, typical, and maximum heat demands are provided as model inputs. The resulting demand represents useful thermal energy and is therefore expressed in kWh of heat. The coefficient of performance (COP) of the heat pump is also drawn from a bounded beta distribution. The COP describes the ratio between the useful heat delivered by the heat pump and its electricity consumption. The total electricity consumption required to provide the drawn heat demand is therefore: \[ E_{\mathrm{HP,run}} = \frac{ Q_{\mathrm{heat,run}} }{ COP } \] where \(Q_{\mathrm{heat,run}}\) is the total heat demand during the simulation period and \(E_{\mathrm{HP,run}}\) is the corresponding heat-pump electricity demand. The temporal distribution of the heat demand is determined using a set of heat-demand profile shapes provided as model input. One profile is randomly selected for each household with a heat pump using user-defined probabilities. The selected profile is resized to match the simulation period and temporal resolution, if necessary, and normalised so that its values sum to one. The heat-pump electricity-demand profile is then calculated as: \[ P_{\mathrm{HP}}(t) = \frac{ Q_{\mathrm{heat,run}} \, s_{\mathrm{heat}}(t) }{ COP \, \Delta t } \] where \(s_{\mathrm{heat}}(t)\) is the normalised heat-demand shape and \(\Delta t\) is the model time-step duration in hours. The resulting profile therefore represents the average electrical power demand of the heat pump in kW at every model time step. The electricity consumed by the heat pump is also included in the household electricity-demand reference used to determine solar-panel production. The reference demand for sizing solar production therefore consists of the basic household electricity demand plus the heat pump's electrical energy demand: \[ E_{\mathrm{reference}} = E_{\mathrm{household,run}} + \frac{ Q_{\mathrm{heat,run}} }{ COP } \] For households without a heat pump, both the heat demand and heat-pump electricity-demand profile are zero.
docs.title: Heat-pump demand

docs.text: Solar panels are included in the household node as a source of electricity production. Whether a household has solar panels is determined stochastically using a user-defined solar-panel adoption rate. Each household therefore has a probability of receiving solar panels equal to the specified adoption rate. For households with solar panels, the total solar production over the simulation period is determined relative to the household electricity demand, including heat-pump electricity demand if a heat pump is present: \[ E_{\mathrm{reference}} = E_{\mathrm{household,run}} + \frac{ Q_{\mathrm{heat,run}} }{ COP } \] The total solar production is then: \[ E_{\mathrm{solar,run}} = E_{\mathrm{reference}} r_{\mathrm{solar}} \] where \(E_{\mathrm{reference}}\) is the household electricity-demand reference over the simulation period and \(r_{\mathrm{solar}}\) is the assumed ratio between solar production and household electricity demand. The model allows this ratio to depend on whether the household also has a home battery. Separate solar-production-to-demand ratios can therefore be provided for households with and without a home battery. This makes it possible to represent a relationship between home-battery ownership and the amount of installed solar generation. The temporal distribution of solar production is determined using a set of solar-production profile shapes provided as model input. One profile variant is randomly selected for each household with solar panels, using user-defined probabilities for the different variants. The selected profile is resized to match the temporal resolution and length of the simulation, if necessary, using the same profile-reshaping procedure as for the basic household demand. The resulting production shape is normalised: \[ \sum_t s_{\mathrm{solar}}(t) = 1 \] The normalised shape is subsequently scaled to the total solar production over the simulation period. The resulting energy per time step is converted from kWh to average power in kW by dividing it by the model time-step duration in hours: \[ P_{\mathrm{solar}}(t) = - \frac{ E_{\mathrm{solar,run}} s_{\mathrm{solar}}(t) }{ \Delta t } \] where \(\Delta t\) is the model time-step duration in hours. Solar production is represented as negative power because the grid convention used in the model considers electricity consumption to be positive and electricity production to be negative. Consequently: \[ -\sum_t P_{\mathrm{solar}}(t)\Delta t = E_{\mathrm{solar,run}} \] For households without solar panels, both solar production and the corresponding power profile are zero. The solar-production profile is subsequently combined with the basic household and heat-pump demand profiles to obtain the household node's initial net non-EV power profile.
docs.title: Solar-panel production

docs.text: Stationary batteries can be present both at household nodes and in combination with EV chargers. Unlike basic household demand, heat-pump demand, and solar production, a stationary battery does not receive a fixed power profile when the residential grid is initialised. Its charging and discharging behaviour depends on the complete power situation, including EV charging, and can therefore only be determined at a later stage. During grid initialisation, the model consequently determines the battery's energy capacity in kWh and its maximum charging and discharging powers in kW. Its charge-level and power-profile series are initially set to zero.
docs.title: Stationary batteries

docs.text: Whether a household has a stationary battery is determined stochastically. Different adoption rates can be specified for households with and without solar panels. For a household that receives a stationary battery, its capacity is based on the household's average daily electricity demand and solar production during the simulation period. Three separate contributions are considered: basic household electricity demand; heat-pump electricity demand; solar-panel production. The duration of the simulation period in days is: \[ D_{\mathrm{run}} = \frac{ N_{\mathrm{steps}} \Delta t }{ 24 } \] where \(N_{\mathrm{steps}}\) is the number of model time steps and \(\Delta t\) is the time-step duration in hours. The capacity associated with basic household demand is: \[ C_{\mathrm{basic}} = \frac{ E_{\mathrm{household,run}} }{ D_{\mathrm{run}} } d_{\mathrm{basic}} \] where \(d_{\mathrm{basic}}\) is the configured number of reserve days for basic household demand. For heat-pump demand, the thermal energy demand is first converted to electrical energy using the heat pump's COP: \[ C_{\mathrm{HP}} = \frac{ Q_{\mathrm{heat,run}} / COP }{ D_{\mathrm{run}} } d_{\mathrm{HP}} \] where \(d_{\mathrm{HP}}\) is the configured number of reserve days for heat-pump electricity demand. The solar-production contribution is: \[ C_{\mathrm{solar}} = \frac{ E_{\mathrm{solar,run}} }{ D_{\mathrm{run}} } d_{\mathrm{solar}} \] where \(d_{\mathrm{solar}}\) is the configured number of reserve days associated with solar production. The total stationary-battery capacity of the household is then: \[ C_{\mathrm{battery}} = C_{\mathrm{basic}} + C_{\mathrm{HP}} + C_{\mathrm{solar}} \] The maximum charging and discharging powers of household stationary batteries are specified directly by the grid parameters.
docs.title: Household stationary batteries

docs.text: EV chargers can also receive a stationary battery. Whether this occurs is determined stochastically using the configured adoption rate for stationary batteries associated with EV chargers. The capacity of such a battery is based on the rated EV-charging power and a configured number of reserve hours: \[ C_{\mathrm{charger\ battery}} = P_{\mathrm{charger}} t_{\mathrm{reserve}} \] This means that a fully charged stationary battery contains enough energy to provide the charger's rated charging power for the configured reserve duration, or a lower power for a correspondingly longer duration. The stationary battery's maximum discharging power is equal to the charger's EV-charging power: \[ P_{\mathrm{battery,discharge,max}} = P_{\mathrm{charger,charge}} \] The stationary battery's maximum charging power is equal to the charger's reverse-power capability: \[ P_{\mathrm{battery,charge,max}} = P_{\mathrm{charger,reverse}} \] The latter represents the reverse power direction through the charger.
docs.title: Stationary batteries associated with EV chargers

docs.text: Stationary batteries are ultimately represented at power-line level. Batteries associated with EV chargers are assigned directly to the line containing the corresponding charger. Household stationary batteries are assigned to the line to which their household node is allocated. For all stationary batteries connected to a line, their capacities and power limits are added: \[ C_{\mathrm{battery,line},i} = \sum_{b \in B_i} C_b \] \[ P_{\mathrm{charge,max},i} = \sum_{b \in B_i} P_{\mathrm{charge,max},b} \] \[ P_{\mathrm{discharge,max},i} = \sum_{b \in B_i} P_{\mathrm{discharge,max},b} \] where \(B_i\) is the set of stationary batteries assigned to line \(i\) . The charge-level and battery-power series are aggregated in the same way. Because no battery dispatch has yet taken place during grid initialisation, these series initially contain zeros. The resulting line-level stationary battery therefore represents the combined stationary-battery capacity and power capability connected to that power line. Its actual charge level and power profile are determined later, when the complete line load, including EV charging, is known. Modelling assumption: The batteries connected to a power line are treated as a single aggregated stationary battery at line level. Their capacities, charging powers, discharging powers, charge levels, and power profiles are added together. This means that the model does not preserve constraints associated with the distribution of stored energy between the individual physical batteries once they have been aggregated.
docs.title: Aggregation of stationary batteries on power lines

docs.text: The household nodes are distributed over the power lines proportionally to their capacities. For each line, the ideal number of household nodes is first calculated from its share of the total line capacity: \[ n_i^* = N_{\mathrm{households}} \frac{P_{\mathrm{line},i}} {\sum_j P_{\mathrm{line},j}} \] Since the number of household nodes assigned to a line must be an integer, these ideal values cannot generally be used directly. The model therefore applies the largest remainder method . First, the ideal number of nodes for each line is rounded down to the nearest integer. This generally leaves a small number of household nodes unassigned. These remaining nodes are assigned, one by one, to the lines with the largest fractional remainders in their ideal allocations. This ensures that the total number of assigned nodes is exactly equal to the number of households, while keeping the distribution as close as possible to proportional to the line capacities. A line may receive no household nodes if the number of households is small relative to the number of lines or its proportional allocation is sufficiently small.
docs.title: Assigning household nodes to lines

docs.text: After determining the number of household nodes connected to each power line, the corresponding non-EV demand profiles are assigned to these lines. The household profiles have already been generated using random draws, so no additional randomisation is applied during this assignment. Instead, the profiles are assigned sequentially according to the previously determined number of nodes per line. For each power line, the non-EV demand profiles of all household nodes assigned to that line are summed to obtain a single line-level non-EV demand profile: \[ P_{\mathrm{non\text{-}EV},i}(t) = \sum_{n \in N_i} P_{\mathrm{non\text{-}EV},n}(t) \] where \(N_i\) is the set of household nodes assigned to line \(i\) . The resulting profile represents the initial non-EV household demand connected to that power line at each time step, before stationary-battery operation is included. At the same time, the stationary batteries belonging to the assigned household nodes are added to the stationary-battery object of the corresponding power line. Their capacities, charging-power limits, discharging-power limits, charge levels, and power profiles are summed. Any stationary batteries associated with EV chargers have already been assigned to their chargers' respective power lines. The resulting power line therefore contains both an initial fixed non-EV power profile and an aggregated stationary battery. The battery power profile is initially zero and is determined later together with EV charging. The eventual power on a line can therefore be represented conceptually as: \[ P_{\mathrm{line},i}(t) = P_{\mathrm{non\text{-}EV},i}(t) + P_{\mathrm{EV},i}(t) + P_{\mathrm{battery},i}(t) \] using the model convention that electricity demand is positive and electricity supply is negative. Battery charging therefore contributes positive power, whereas battery discharging contributes negative power.
docs.title: Assigning non-EV demand to lines

docs.text: Matching EV demand to the residential grid After EV charging has been simulated, the resulting charging demand is matched to the residential power lines to which the EV users are connected. For each power line, the model considers all EV users assigned to that line. Only charging taking place at home is included in the residential-grid demand. Charging at other locations is not assigned to the residential power line. The home-charging demand of all EV users connected to a line is summed for each timestep: \[ P_{\mathrm{EV},t} = \sum_i P_{\mathrm{EV},i,t} \] where \(P_{\mathrm{EV},i,t}\) is the power drawn from the grid by EV user \(i\) at home during timestep \(t\) . This EV demand is combined with the existing non-EV demand of the power line: \[ P_{\mathrm{total},t} = P_{\mathrm{non-EV},t} + P_{\mathrm{EV},t} \] The total demand is compared with the capacity of the power line. The line is considered overloaded when: \[ P_{\mathrm{total},t} > P_{\mathrm{capacity}} \] For an overloaded timestep, the additional capacity required is calculated as: \[ P_{\mathrm{additional},t} = P_{\mathrm{total},t} - P_{\mathrm{capacity}} \] If the capacity is not exceeded, the additional capacity required is zero. For example, consider a power line with a capacity of 100 kW. If non-EV demand is 70 kW and home EV charging contributes another 45 kW, total demand is 115 kW: \[ 70 + 45 = 115\ \mathrm{kW} \] The power line is therefore overloaded. The additional capacity required is: \[ 115 - 100 = 15\ \mathrm{kW} \] The resulting EV demand, overload status, and additional capacity requirement are stored for every timestep in the power line's EV-demand-matching DataFrame. These results can subsequently be aggregated across power lines to calculate the residential grid-congestion statistics. Residential grid congestion statistics Residential grid congestion is evaluated for each power line and timestep. A power line is considered overloaded when its total electricity demand exceeds its available capacity. Two related but distinct measures of congestion are calculated: Number of overloaded lines For every timestep, the number of power lines exceeding their capacity is counted. Because multiple lines can be overloaded simultaneously, this value can be larger than one. The average number of overloaded lines per timestep is calculated over the simulation. Timesteps with an overload A timestep is considered congested when at least one power line exceeds its capacity. The proportion of congested timesteps therefore represents how often residential grid congestion occurs, irrespective of how many lines are overloaded simultaneously. For example, consider four timesteps with the following numbers of overloaded lines: Timestep Overloaded lines At least one overloaded 1 0 No 2 1 Yes 3 2 Yes 4 0 No There are three line-overload occurrences in total. The average number of overloaded lines per timestep is therefore 3 / 4 = 0.75 . However, an overload occurs during only two of the four timesteps. The proportion of timesteps with at least one overloaded line is therefore 2 / 4 = 0.50 . Both measures are also calculated separately for each hour of the day (0–23). This makes it possible to identify both when congestion occurs most frequently and when multiple power lines tend to be overloaded simultaneously.

docs.text: Monte Carlo simulations The model uses Monte Carlo simulation to represent variation in model inputs and behaviour. Instead of assigning every modelled user or process the same fixed values, selected parameters can be drawn from probability distributions. The Monte Carlo configuration determines whether these random draws are reproducible. Separate random-number generators are used for different parts of the model, while bounded beta distributions can be used to draw values around specified typical values. Monte Carlo configuration The MonteCarlo class contains the configuration used to initialise the random-number generation for a model run. It contains two parameters: use_seed determines whether the model uses a fixed seed. seed specifies the fixed seed used when seeding is enabled. When use_seed is True , the configured seed produces the same sequence of random draws each time the model is run. Provided that the rest of the model is deterministic, this makes the complete model run reproducible. Reproducible random draws make it possible to compare model configurations without introducing unrelated differences in random sampling. For example, the effect of changing a charging parameter can be examined while retaining the same randomly generated characteristics and mobility behaviour. When use_seed is False , the configured value of seed is not used. NumPy then supplies non-deterministic entropy to initialise the seed sequence. Repeated model runs can consequently produce different sequences of random draws. Independent random-number generators The RandomGenerators class contains separate NumPy random-number generators for different parts of the model: define is used when defining model inputs and characteristics. mobility is used for random processes related to mobility. charging is used for random processes related to vehicle charging. transformers is used for random processes related to transformers and power lines = households is used for randome processes related to household consumption (outside elelectric vehicles), including heat pumps, home batteries, and solr panels. Separating the random-number generators prevents a change in one part of the model from unnecessarily shifting the random-number stream used by another part. For example, adding an extra charging-related draw should not change the mobility draws merely because both processes would otherwise consume values from the same random-number sequence. The generators are created by the RandomGenerators.create_generators() method. This method first creates a NumPy SeedSequence from the configured Monte Carlo seed. It then uses SeedSequence.spawn() to create three child seed sequences, one for each random-number generator. When seeding is enabled, the same root seed produces the same child seed sequences and therefore the same three random-number streams. The streams remain separate but are reproducible as a group. When seeding is disabled, the root seed sequence is initialised using non-deterministic entropy. Drawing bounded parameter values The draw_beta_value() function draws a value within a specified range. The function requires a minimum value, a typical value, a maximum value, a random-number generator, and a beta-distribution shape parameter. The input values must satisfy: minimum <= typical <= maximum The returned value is therefore bounded by minimum and maximum . The typical value defines the central value around which the draws are distributed. A bounded distribution is useful for model parameters for which values outside the specified range would be physically impossible, behaviourally implausible, or inconsistent with the scenario definition. Beta distribution and transformation The function first draws a value from a symmetric beta distribution: Beta(shape, shape) This produces a value between zero and one. Because both beta shape parameters are equal, the distribution is symmetric around 0.5 . The beta draw is subsequently transformed in two parts: A beta draw between 0 and 0.5 is mapped to the interval from minimum to typical . A beta draw between 0.5 and 1 is mapped to the interval from typical to maximum . For draws at or below 0.5 , the transformation is: minimum + 2 * draw * (typical - minimum) For draws above 0.5 , the transformation is: typical + 2 * (draw - 0.5) * (maximum - typical) This piecewise transformation allows the typical value to be positioned anywhere between the minimum and maximum. The distance from the minimum to the typical value does not need to equal the distance from the typical value to the maximum. Interpretation of the typical value The typical value is a median of the resulting distribution. When minimum < typical < maximum , half of the generated values are below the typical value and half are above it. This does not necessarily make the typical value the arithmetic mean of the resulting distribution. When the intervals below and above the typical value have different widths, the resulting distribution is asymmetric in terms of the modelled parameter. The typical value remains the median, but the mean may lie above or below it. For example, consider: minimum = 10 typical = 20 maximum = 50 Half of the draws are located between 10 and 20, while the other half are located between 20 and 50. The upper half covers a wider interval. Consequently, the mean of the resulting values will be greater than 20 even though 20 is the median. This makes it possible to specify a typical value independently of the width of the ranges on either side of it. Effect of the shape parameter The shape parameter controls how strongly draws are concentrated around the typical value. Values greater than 1 produce a concentration around the typical value. As shape increases, the symmetric beta distribution becomes increasingly concentrated around 0.5 . After transformation, this results in a stronger concentration of draws around typical . A shape value of 1 produces a uniform beta draw between zero and one. Half of these draws are mapped uniformly to the interval between minimum and typical , and the other half are mapped uniformly to the interval between typical and maximum . The resulting distribution over the full range is therefore only uniform when typical is halfway between minimum and maximum . Values below 1 increasingly favour the minimum and maximum. The underlying beta distribution becomes increasingly concentrated near zero and one, which correspond to the minimum and maximum after transformation. The shape parameter must be greater than zero. Validation Before drawing a value, draw_beta_value() verifies that the shape parameter is greater than zero and that the minimum, typical, and maximum values are correctly ordered. A ValueError is raised when: shape <= 0 A ValueError is also raised when the following condition is not satisfied: minimum <= typical <= maximum These checks prevent invalid beta-distribution parameters and incorrectly specified value ranges from being silently accepted. Fixed and degenerate ranges The function also supports cases in which two or all three of the range values are equal. For example: minimum = typical < maximum means that beta draws in the lower half of the distribution all result in the typical value, while draws in the upper half are distributed between the typical value and the maximum. Similarly: minimum < typical = maximum causes draws in the upper half to result in the typical value, while draws in the lower half are distributed between the minimum and typical values. When: minimum = typical = maximum the returned value is always equal to this fixed value. Importantly, a random beta draw is still performed in this final case even though it cannot affect the returned value. Maintaining the random-number stream Performing a random draw when minimum == maximum is deliberate. Skipping the draw only when a parameter has a fixed value would shift all subsequent draws from the same random-number generator. This could cause later model results to change merely because an earlier parameter happened to have a fixed value, even when those later results should otherwise be independent of that parameter. By consuming one beta draw on every call, including when minimum == maximum , the position within the random-number stream is preserved relative to another run that calls the function at the same point with a non-degenerate range. This makes controlled comparisons between model configurations easier because making this parameter fixed does not, by itself, shift subsequent draws from the same generator. Reproducibility A fixed Monte Carlo seed makes the random-number streams reproducible. Complete model results are reproducible when stochastic operations consistently use the provided generators and the remainder of the calculation behaves deterministically. Random operations should therefore use the appropriate generator from RandomGenerators : definition-related draws use define ; mobility-related draws use mobility ; charging-related draws use charging . Keeping these random streams separate also limits the effect of changes within one part of the model. A change in the number of charging draws, for example, can alter subsequent draws from the charging generator, but does not shift the sequence produced by the mobility or define generators. For reproducible simulations, random draws should consistently use these generators rather than an independent or global random-number state.

docs.text: The model uses Monte Carlo simulation to represent variation in model inputs and behaviour. Instead of assigning every modelled user or process the same fixed values, selected parameters can be drawn from probability distributions. The Monte Carlo configuration determines whether these random draws are reproducible. Separate random-number generators are used for different parts of the model, while bounded beta distributions can be used to draw values around specified typical values.
docs.title: Monte Carlo simulations

docs.text: The MonteCarlo class contains the configuration used to initialise the random-number generation for a model run. It contains two parameters: use_seed determines whether the model uses a fixed seed. seed specifies the fixed seed used when seeding is enabled. When use_seed is True , the configured seed produces the same sequence of random draws each time the model is run. Provided that the rest of the model is deterministic, this makes the complete model run reproducible. Reproducible random draws make it possible to compare model configurations without introducing unrelated differences in random sampling. For example, the effect of changing a charging parameter can be examined while retaining the same randomly generated characteristics and mobility behaviour. When use_seed is False , the configured value of seed is not used. NumPy then supplies non-deterministic entropy to initialise the seed sequence. Repeated model runs can consequently produce different sequences of random draws.
docs.title: Monte Carlo configuration

docs.text: The RandomGenerators class contains separate NumPy random-number generators for different parts of the model: define is used when defining model inputs and characteristics. mobility is used for random processes related to mobility. charging is used for random processes related to vehicle charging. transformers is used for random processes related to transformers and power lines = households is used for randome processes related to household consumption (outside elelectric vehicles), including heat pumps, home batteries, and solr panels. Separating the random-number generators prevents a change in one part of the model from unnecessarily shifting the random-number stream used by another part. For example, adding an extra charging-related draw should not change the mobility draws merely because both processes would otherwise consume values from the same random-number sequence. The generators are created by the RandomGenerators.create_generators() method. This method first creates a NumPy SeedSequence from the configured Monte Carlo seed. It then uses SeedSequence.spawn() to create three child seed sequences, one for each random-number generator. When seeding is enabled, the same root seed produces the same child seed sequences and therefore the same three random-number streams. The streams remain separate but are reproducible as a group. When seeding is disabled, the root seed sequence is initialised using non-deterministic entropy.

docs.text: Scenario file description The models runs through a series of scenarios. For each scenario, you need to create a scenario file in the scenarios/your_case folder (or use a variant ). This page describes the elements of the scenario file (your_scenario.toml). run Run parameters give the elements to produce the time tags of the run range. use_day_types_in_charge_computing If set to true, the charging computations will be done per day type rather than for all days of the run, which fastens the computations in the charging module . If set to false, the model will compute each day separately, which is considerably slower. start This part gives the year, month, day, hour, and minute of the start of the computations. It is best to set this to a day hour start for consistency and then cut off the start for display (see below). For example, start on 31/12/2019 at 05:00 if your day start hour is 05:00 and if you want to show results starting on 1/1/2020 at 00:00. end This part gives the year, month, day, hour, and minute of the end of the computations. Note that the end time tag is not included in the run, so put 1/1/2021 at 00:00 if you want to compute for 2020. display_start This is the first time tag you want to show in your end results. display_end This is the first time tag that does not appear in your displayed results. frequency The time frequency of the run (size and type). For the type, use 'H' for hours, 'min' for minutes, 'S' for seconds, 'D' for days. For more info and other types, see here . The current model uses hourly (so 1 and 'h'). Changing that might require some adjustments in the code. display frequency The frequency of the displayed values can be different than the frequency of the computations. In the current version, this needs to be the same or less frequent than the computation frequency above. extra_downloads This is to decide if you want to dowload some files (note that this concerns the currently inactive weather module). download_weather_data Put true if you want to download the weather data. In principle, you only to do this once, unless you add years and/or areas make_weather_database Put true if you want to remake the weather database. In principle, you only to do this once, unless you add years and/or areas. Note that this refers to other years ans areas than the weather download. download_EV_tool_data Put true if you want to download the data from the EV tool by geootab This should only be needed once and is independentr of the case. locations You can modify existing locations or create new ones by copying exisiting ones (copy everything under '[locations.code]', where code is the name of your location). You need to have all the elements below. vehicle This is the name of the vehicle that goes to that location. This name needs to match the scenario's vehicle name (in vehicle ) for the location to be included in the scenario. The reason for this check is to avoid including unnecessary locations (a user could put all locations for all vehicles in their scenario files so that they could copy the whole list between scenarios without having to filter locations by hand). If a location is used by different vehicles, simply create one location per vehicle (e.g. stadium_car and stadium_bus). connectivity This is a (float) number between 0 and 1 that gives us the probability that a vehicle is connected to a charger when it is at this location (essentially, it is the ratio between parking places with a charger and the total amount of parkin places). charging_power The available charging power (in kW). charger_efficiency This is a (float) number between 0 and 1 that gives us the charger efficiency. docs.text: Scenario file description The models runs through a series of scenarios. For each scenario, you need to create a scenario file in the scenarios/your_case folder (or use a variant ). This page describes the elements of the scenario file (your_scenario.toml). run Run parameters give the elements to produce the time tags of the run range. use_day_types_in_charge_computing If set to true, the charging computations will be done per day type rather than for all days of the run, which fastens the computations. start This part gives the year, month, day, hour, and minute of the start of the computations. It is best to set this to a day hour start for consistency and then cut off the start for display (see below). For example, start on 31/12/2019 at 05:00 if your day start hour is 05:00 and if you want to show results starting on 1/1/2020 at 00:00. end This part gives the year, month, day, hour, and minute of the end of the computations. Note that the end time tag is not included in the run, so put 1/1/2021 at 00:00 if you want to compute for 2020. display_start This is the first time tag you want to show in your end results. display_end This is the first time tag that does not appear in your displayed results. frequency The time frequency of the run (size and type). For the type, use 'H' for hours, 'min' for minutes, 'S' for seconds, 'D' for days. For more info and other types, see here . The current model uses hourly (so 1 and 'h'). Changing that might require some adjustments in the code. display frequency The frequency of the displayed values can be different than the frequency of the compuatations. In the current version, this needs to be the same or less frequent than the computation frequencey above. extra_downloads This is to decide if you want to dowload some files (note that this concerns the currently inactive weather module). locations vehicle connectivity charging_power charger_efficiency latitude longitude charging_price charging_desirability An indicator (0-1) of how much people like to charge at this location percentage_in_location_at_run_start If filling it directly instead of computing it (controlled by compute_start_location_split in mobility_module below) vehicle_discharge_power proportion_of_discharge_to_network time_modulation_factors Starts at midinight legs vehicle distance duration hour_in_day_factors This factor adds a correction to the vehicle consumption that depends on the hour in day (the first is for 00:00 to 00:59, the last for 23:00 to 23:59). Note that these are actual hours, not hours in the user day (which can start and end at other moments than midnight). This is used to take into account things like traffic jams. The default value is 1. locations road_type_mix Give the road type mix We need a value for each of the road_types (see above in [transport_factors]) If the road type does not occur in the leg, simply put 0 Note that the total should be 1 (there are not checks to ensure this, so you need to make sure you do this correctly) road_types = ['highway', 'city'] mix vehicle These parameters define the scenario's vehicle. If you want profiles for several vehicles, run separate scenarios. name This is the name of the vehicle, which will be checked to see if trips and locations are actually declared. base_location not relevant for cars yearly_kilometrage Not relevant for cars, as it is built bottom-up kilometers_column_for_consumption use_weighted battery_capacity solar_panel_size_kWp base_consumption_per_km electricity_kWh = 0.76 gasoline_litres = 0.3399 diesel_litres = 0.2917 hydrogen_kg = 0.0398 CNG_kg = 0.2415 LNG_kg = 0.2415 trips vehicle legs time_between_legs This is the time spent at each interim location (same units as used general) percentage_station_users start_probabilities repeated_sequence repetition_amounts time_between_repetitions mobility_module day_start_hour This parameter defines the start of the day for the scenario. It is chosen so that there are no movements during that hour number. It represents the shift from midnight, so a day start hour of 5 means that the day starts at hour 5 (i.e. 05.00). The idea is to choose an hour that is logical for the users/matches their patterns. This is connected to the day types , as a given day will correspond to a day type. For example, the hours between 00:00 and 05:00 on a Saturday belong to the Thursday before and are as such on a week day (as opposed to a weekend day). compute_start_location_split day_types mobility_quantities battery_space_shift_quantities location_connections_headers mobility_index_names kilometers_driven_headers holiday_weeks number_of_holiday_weeks We need to provide the number of holliday weeks seprately, as counting the elements of the list above might not work, such as when the above list contains weeks 1 and 53 (which just represent the fact that years don't necessarily start and/or end at the start/end of a week). holiday_departures_in_weekend_week_numbers holiday_returns_in_weekend_week_numbers work_hours_in_a_work_day hours_worked_per_work_week hours_in_a_standard_work_week percentage_working_on_a_work_week worked_hours_per_year leisure_trips_per_weekend leisure_trips_per_week_outside_weekends maximal_fill_percentage_leisure_trips_on_non_work_weekdays weekday_leisure_trips percentage_of_weekday_leisure_trips_on_a_work_day weekend_trips_per_year holiday_trips_taken time_spent_at_holiday_destination trips_per_day_type For vehicles other than cars, we assume that there is one trip per day type. This is where we match the trips to their day type transport_factors road_types weights weather weather_factors_table_root_name source_data start_year end_year quantities raw_data_folder The following define the area over which the raw weather data will be downloaded. The corresponding in the processed weather database is below. latitude_min latitude_max longitude_min longitude_max processed_data raw_data_folder processed_folder weather_database_file_name chunk_size This parameter is there to avoid issues when writing a too large DataFrame at once (instead, we split it into chunks). quantities KELVIN_TO_CELSIUS quantity_tags quantity_processed_names cumulative_quantity_processed_names cumulative_quantities queries_for_cumulative_quantities temperature_quantities processed_index_tags These define the area of the processed data in the weather database latitude_min latitude_max longitude_min longitude_max coordinate_step EV_tool Parameters for the EV tool data from geotab EV_tool_url user_agent efficiency_curve_script_index data_splitter file_name groupfile_name folder efficiency_factor_column_name charging price_reaction_exponent desirability_reaction_exponent charging_sessions resolution
